extraction.name: FLEURS
extraction.description: FLEURS (Few-shot Learning Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech) is an n-way parallel speech dataset in 102 languages built on top of the machine translation FLoRes-101 benchmark, with approximately 12 hours of speech supervision per language. It contains spoken utterances recorded by native speakers for aligned sentences across 102 languages, designed for speech recognition, speech language identification, translation, and cross-modal retrieval.
extraction.creator: Alexis Conneau, Min Ma, Simran Khanuja, Yu Zhang, Vera Axelrod, Siddharth Dalmia, Jason Riesa, Clara Rivera, Ankur Bapna
extraction.inLanguage: 102 languages including Afrikaans, Amharic, Arabic, Armenian, Assamese, Asturian, Azerbaijani, Belarusian, Bengali, Bosnian, Bulgarian, Burmese, Cantonese Chinese, Catalan, Cebuano, Croatian, Czech, Danish, Dutch, English, Estonian, Filipino, Finnish, French, Fula, Galician, Ganda, Georgian, German, Greek, Gujarati, Hausa, Hebrew, Hindi, Hungarian, Icelandic, Igbo, Indonesian, Irish, Italian, Japanese, Javanese, Kabuverdianu, Kamba, Kannada, Kazakh, Khmer, Korean, Kyrgyz, Lao, Latvian, Lingala, Lithuanian, Luo, Luxembourgish, Macedonian, Malay, Malayalam, Maltese, Mandarin Chinese, Maori, Marathi, Mongolian, Nepali, Northern Sotho, Norwegian, Nyanja, Occitan, Oriya, Oromo, Pashto, Persian, Polish, Portuguese, Punjabi, Romanian, Russian, Serbian, Shona, Sindhi, Slovak, Slovenian, Somali, Sorani Kurdish, Spanish, Swahili, Swedish, Tajik, Tamil, Telugu, Thai, Turkish, Ukrainian, Umbundu, Urdu, Uzbek, Vietnamese, Welsh, Wolof, Xhosa, Yoruba, Zulu
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Starting from the FLoRes-101 dev and devtest sets (2009 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia translated into 101 languages by human translators), the sentences were split into train (1509), dev (150), and test (350) splits. For each sentence across the 102 languages, three recordings were collected from three different native speakers with a sex ratio balance of at least 30/70% when possible. Audio recordings were sampled at 16kHz and kept as-is from quiet or noisy environments without data augmentations. Disjoint speakers were maintained between train/dev and test sets.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: In the first version of the dataset, about 21.5% of the sentences are missing because none of the three recordings were validated. The authors plan to fill these gaps in future versions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: FLoRes-101 benchmark sentences extracted from English Wikipedia and translated by human translators, recorded by native human speakers.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: NFC and FST normalization were applied to each sentence, along with lower-casing, punctuation removal and normalization. Words were split into characters, and the token ' ' was defined as word boundaries. All audio segments are within 30 seconds and sampled at 16kHz.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: After recording, each recording was evaluated by additional workers to assess whether the recording corresponds to the input sentence. Invalid recordings were discarded, leaving between zero and three recordings per sentence in the final dataset.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Recordings were evaluated to determine whether the spoken utterance corresponded to the input sentence; any invalid recordings were discarded.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Between zero and three recordings per sentence in the final dataset (evaluated by additional workers from initial three recordings).
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Native speakers of the respective 102 languages, with an imposed sex ratio balance of at least 30/70% when possible.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors plan to fill the 21.5% missing sentence gaps in future versions of the dataset.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Sex (gender balance of at least 30/70% recorded when possible), voice recordings, and native language.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Aims to enable speech technology in more languages, catalyze research in low-resource speech understanding, and build speech technologies for everyone.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Performance disparities exist across language families and geographical groups: Western European and Eastern European groups show much lower error rates compared to Sub-Saharan African and South Asian groups, largely due to pre-existing disparities in pre-training data availability.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: In the first version, approximately 21.5% of sentences are missing due to rejected recordings; performance degrades significantly on unseen languages without pre-training data and on mixed writing systems or scripts absent from pre-training tokenizers.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech Language Identification (Speech LangID), Speech-to-Text Translation, Speech-to-Speech Translation, Multilingual Speech-to-Speech Retrieval, and Speech-to-Text Retrieval.
